items.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
items.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
items.story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
items.content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

items.title: $γ$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence
items.summary: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.

items.title: HookEvo: A Framework for Coordinated Plugin Evolution on Hook-Enabled Agent Runtimes
items.summary: Repairing failures in tool-using agents can require coordinated changes to how the harness interprets tool receipts, assembles context, and checks actions. We introduce HookEvo, a framework that uses an existing agent runtime's lifecycle hooks to evolve task-specific harnesses. We instantiate HookEvo on DeepSeek Harness. In each round, a separate improver diagnoses failures from execution traces and proposes a candidate. HookEvo evaluates the candidate against the current harness on matched tasks and carries the retained version into the next round. A single candidate can jointly edit executable plugin handlers and the state they share within a task, allowing a tool receipt to inform context and control a later action. Using a frozen Qwen3-4B executor, the selected harnesses lead the reported Qwen3-4B comparisons, achieving 95.41% on ALFWorld, 70.56% on DBBench, 48.17% on WebShop, and 41.67% on OSBench. Across three improvers and three edit scopes, from skill text to single-component and coordinated executable edits, GPT-6.1 Sol shows the largest average gain from the broadest scope. Our code is available at https://huangshengzebluesky.github.io/hookevo/.

items.title: Can Vision-Language Models Synthesize Executable Game-Playing Programs?
items.summary: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have endowed multimodal agents with increasingly strong visual perception and long-horizon reasoning capabilities, making VLM-based autonomous game playing feasible. Existing game benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can select appropriate actions from the current visual state across different scenarios and games. However, most of them adopt a step-by-step interaction paradigm where the current visual observation is sent to the agent before each action. In practical deployment, this paradigm introduces two fundamental limitations: the game loop must wait for model inference, making real-time interaction impractical, and repeated VLM calls incur substantial cost. Therefore, we propose PlayScriptBench, a script-based game benchmark that evaluates whether VLMs can synthesize an executable game-playing program from game states. This setting jointly evaluates visual grounding, understanding of game dynamics, long-horizon strategic reasoning, and executable program synthesis, providing a more comprehensive assessment of game-playing agents. To support more tractable evaluation for current general-purpose VLMs, we further introduce a four-stage pipeline --- Explore, Perception, API Construction, and Strategy Composition --- that decomposes controller synthesis into game exploration, state perception, interface construction, and strategic control, enabling agents to progressively construct an executable program. Experiments on 16 games spanning 4 genres show that even strong VLMs struggle on our benchmark, revealing a substantial gap between passive visual game understanding and executable closed-loop game control. These results establish script-based controller synthesis as a complementary direction for benchmarking VLM-based game-playing agents.

items.title: Why agent governance starts with observability
items.summary: A strong AI agent governance strategy
items.story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
items.content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective. items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

Change What to do PR
Model Runner V1 removed Remove VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor. #63373
Default --block-size is 64 (was 16) Pass --block-size 16 to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. #63231
Extensible KV cache on by default; gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 In most cases it's now best to not set gpu_memory_utilization. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. #56492
ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. -rocm72 is no longer published. #61939
huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 required Also requires tokenizers >= 0.23.3 and timm >= 1.0.30. #64779
QuTLASS / fp_quant removed fp_quant checkpoints no longer load. #65230
Marlin W4A8 removed Use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG instead of VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE. #65542
Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed — #64287

All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in the full changelog.

New models

Model Notes PR
Mistral Large 4 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. #64534
MiniMax-M3.1-Flash Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft #64111
NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and /v1/audio/transcriptions #64282
Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview BF16 and NVFP4, ripple reasoning and tool parsers #65745
Zyphra ZAYA1 ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview #65302
Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 DASH sparse attention #64016
Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio #65826, #65827, #65828
NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 ASR and X↔En translation #64215
Ming3-ASR #63585
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin #65005

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

Performance

Improvement Hardware Gain PR
Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen 4×GB200 up to 1.95× decode #65152
GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE NVIDIA 1.6× output throughput vs DEP4 #60895
Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) GB300 1.5× single-stream decode #64077
Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) GB200 GLM-5.3 TTFT 1.24–1.40× faster at 32K–128K #63956
KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) GB300 1.34–1.59× decode attention #63638
Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) NVIDIA 3.0–8.8% lower decode ITL #51012
FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark 8×MI355X +35–57% interactivity at conc. 1–8 #63440

AMD ROCm

  • Release images and wheels are ROCm 10.0 only (#61939).
  • MoRI EPv2 via --all2all-backend mori (#61361).
  • Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435).
  • TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418).

Serving and operations

  • Checkpoint/restore (CRIU + cuda-checkpoint) through /checkpoint/prepare, /checkpoint/status and /checkpoint/restore, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570).
  • Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down: dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370).
  • Best-effort NUMA binding on by default (#61258).
  • Opt-in cache-aware admission ordering (#54625).
  • Rust frontend: stateless Responses API (#63902) and n > 1 (#65625).

Install

Python wheels

Platform Install

CUDA 13.0 (uv) uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto
ROCm 10.0 pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100
XPU uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match

The Assets section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels.

    • fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540).
    • DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996).

items.title: claude-code v2.1.326
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while agent teams are enabled; if you already turned it on, sessions with teams on now start in Code Mode
  • Added a startup warning when an --allowedTools, --disallowedTools or --tools value has an entry that doesn't look like a complete rule
  • Added a message explaining why MCP servers stop loading when an administrator adds managed-mcp.json during a session
  • Added a row to /status that says when your provider or an environment variable such as DISABLE_TELEMETRY turns features off
  • Added a note in /plugin and claude plugin list when a malformed plugin.json field such as author or homepage is ignored
  • Added Ctrl+O to show hidden startup notices
  • Added a hint in the empty prompt that says what to do after a request fails
  • Added an esc to stop footer hint in a subagent's view where Esc would stop it
  • Added OTEL_RESOURCE_INCLUDE_HOST to include host.name and host.id in OpenTelemetry resource attributes (off by default)
  • Added overflowX="scroll" on a mod's Box, and maxLines and wrap="clip" on its Text
  • Fixed cp of a file being refused when only its source was covered by an Edit deny rule
  • Fixed Bash commands that delete or overwrite files (find -delete, cat a > b, sort -o) being summed up in the transcript as a search or a read
  • Fixed a misleading "Dangerous rm operation" warning in the Bash permission prompt on some commands with no rm that Claude Code can't read reliably
  • Fixed background sessions losing the LLM gateway your shell exported after a crash, after a reopen from another folder, or when the background service lacks it: they now stop before any model request
  • Fixed the background service ending your own processes, such as an SSH login, when a process number on its list had been reused by another user's process
  • Fixed rules added in /permissions or at a main-conversation tool prompt, and /add-dir folders, looking saved when the settings file couldn't be written; the terminal now warns and names it
  • Fixed a failed MCP headersHelper, or one not run in an untrusted folder, making other sessions start without that server, for most servers with no stored OAuth refresh token
  • Fixed managed settings with certain key names stopping Claude Code from starting or affecting other managed files
  • Fixed settings files with values nested thousands of levels deep crashing Claude Code or applying only some of the time; values past 64 levels are now dropped with a warning
  • Fixed a settings file saved with an error mid-session being skipped silently; a warning now names the file
  • Fixed the subagent model set in managed settings not applying in Claude Desktop's Code tab; it now overrides your own, as in a terminal, unless those settings also pick a provider or gateway
  • Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when the home or config directory is reached through a symlink into /net and sandbox settings deny reads of it
  • Fixed empty placeholder files, including .git/config.lock, sometimes being left in the project on Linux when Claude Code was stopped during a sandboxed command
  • Fixed Up then Enter answering Yes at the folder trust prompt shown under an already trusted parent folder
  • Fixed an extra Enter at the end of setup accepting the offer to make auto mode the default
  • Fixed a message typed over the startup auto mode offer being lost, and its Enter accepting the offer
  • Fixed a note typed on a permission prompt being sent to Claude after Tab had hidden it
  • Fixed PreToolUse hooks in managed settings leaving no OpenTelemetry tool_decision event or permission_denials entry when they refused a direct tool call
  • Fixed letters typed over /sandbox or a delete question in /permissions moving the selection
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing recent turns after a crash when the previous turn ended with an empty reply
  • Fixed resumed sessions losing earlier conversation history when Claude Code ran low on memory
  • Fixed a re-sent file overwriting Claude's changed copy in Remote Control and cloud sessions on Linux with no feature flags loaded: the copy moves to a .kept- folder, or the new file isn't saved
  • Fixed a background session being killed and its request lost when you opened, stopped or removed the older session whose conversation it had resumed
  • Fixed claude purge hiding its prompts when stdout is redirected, where one unseen Enter could delete a project's data; they now show on the terminal
  • Fixed the spend limit menu removing the monthly limit without asking when Backspace and Enter were pressed as it opened
  • Fixed /rewind restoring only some files after running /branch twice while a slow backup copy was still running
  • Fixed /rewind saying "No code changes" when a shell command changed files it can't restore; a turn whose changes weren't tracked now reads "Code changes unknown"
  • Fixed /rewind: Esc now cancels its summary, its list shows more than one past prompt in fullscreen, and a long prompt no longer hides its warning about losing later file changes
  • Fixed Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D twice in /skills quitting Claude Code and dropping changes; it now saves and closes the panel
  • Fixed the usage limit menu erasing your draft and opening while you were typing
  • Fixed pasted text and images being dropped when ↑ recalls a draft cleared with Esc Esc
  • Fixed an edited typed answer to Claude's question sending the old text when you moved on without pressing Enter
  • Fixed going back to a question you answered from its list putting the cursor on the first option, where Enter replaced your answer
  • Fixed /feedback and /bug sending the report when you typed a space on the confirmation screen, and losing the typed report after Ctrl+O or Ctrl+Z
  • Fixed a prompt typed after --add-dir, --allowedTools or another list option being dropped without a message
  • Fixed /plan <description> ignoring the description when plan mode was already on
  • Fixed valid PDFs being dropped from the conversation after the API rejected a different PDF read in the same batch
  • Fixed a session ending after a single failed memory allocation while drawing the screen
  • Fixed compaction on Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry, and with telemetry turned off, sometimes replying to one of your messages instead of summarizing, or leaving Claude's last reply out of the summary
  • Fixed image-heavy sessions on Vertex AI getting stuck on a 400 error about the request size exceeding a 30 MB limit, instead of compacting and retrying
  • Fixed an error when max_tokens exceeded the model's limit: Claude Code now retries the request with the maximum the Anthropic API reports
  • Fixed grep in the Bash tool silently skipping some text files
  • Fixed a crashed Node or Python hook showing only the first line of its stack trace; the error is now shown, and Ctrl+O shows up to 10,000 characters of the output
  • Fixed /goal clear or a new /goal not sticking when typed while Stop hooks were running and background work was still in progress
  • Fixed the automatic session recap being sent after a reply billed to usage credits; /recap still works
  • Fixed auto mode staying on its local classifier, which counts toward usage, because of a stale saved value, such as one from an older Claude Code
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your Claude subscription login when the browser sign-in used your Claude plan instead of a Console organization
  • Fixed /login ending on "Login successful" while an approved ANTHROPIC_API_KEY was still used; it now says requests still use the key
  • Fixed "Not logged in" staying after turning on the API key in /config; "Not logged in", /login and /status now name an unused ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  • Fixed claude auth logout leaving credentials behind, and token refresh failing, when only a Console profile's credentials are on a drive that rejects folder timestamps
  • Fixed a past conversation resumed from agent view being sent on the background service's sign-in when the service doesn't have the terminal's API key or token
  • Fixed model requests failing on a one-off authentication error (401) in Claude Desktop's Code tab: they are now sent once more first
  • Fixed forceLoginOrgUUID and forceRemoteSettingsRefresh startup errors telling you to sign in again when a network block page (HTTP 403) was the cause
  • Fixed claude auth login not showing a pasted sign-in code, so a wrong paste couldn't be seen or corrected before Enter
  • Fixed /login and claude setup-token showing nothing after you submit a pasted code; they now show "Finishing sign-in…"
  • Fixed Esc doing nothing while the first-run sign-in waits for the browser or a pasted code; it now goes back one screen
  • Fixed /logout in fullscreen mode exiting without leaving the logged-out message on screen
  • Fixed the shell prompt being drawn over the last screen after quitting with Ctrl+C or Ctrl+D at a sign-in or first-run step
  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice doing nothing on the first-run theme choice, and freezing the terminal on setup screens or a background session at its startup question
  • Fixed your OFF answer to the updated terms being replaced when keys were typed while it was saving, at startup and in /privacy-settings
  • Fixed the /privacy-settings toggle sometimes saving the opposite of what the screen showed on a quick double press, changing your setting on keys pressed after Esc, and not saying when a save failed
  • Fixed /privacy-settings saving your choice on the wrong account after signing in to a different account in another terminal
  • Fixed /privacy-settings saying "set to true" when you picked OFF right after ON
  • Fixed skills and slash commands failing to load in Code Mode under auto mode when an inline ! command needs approval; Claude is now asked to run it
  • Fixed background subagents started in Code Mode failing when they preload a skill with an inline ! command
  • Fixed mods being unable to use Bash, Read and other tools through $.tool.call and $.tool.check in Code Mode
  • Fixed parallel MCP tool calls reading another call's saved result when two long results arrived in the same millisecond (#105138)
  • Fixed tool search sometimes loading another MCP server's tool when asked for a tool by its exact name; you may be asked again for that tool
  • Fixed MCP prompts disappearing when two servers have nearly identical names
  • Fixed a tool call to an MCP server that an SDK host had just removed reconnecting to it, or reporting that it needs authentication
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a remote MCP server's question was declined when the server then failed the tool call
  • Fixed MCP tools with a root anyOf or oneOf showing Claude only the first branch's form of an argument; text such as 42 can now arrive as a number where another branch takes one
  • Fixed Claude not being told when an approved MCP resource tool was unavailable after a cloud session's worker was replaced
  • Fixed /mcp not showing why a local (stdio) MCP server failed to start
  • Fixed Esc doing nothing while an MCP server reconnects: Esc, or Ctrl+C pressed twice, now closes the wait and the reconnect continues in the background
  • Fixed Enable in /mcp showing no progress for a slow server, and a second Enter disabling it again
  • Fixed claude mcp add-json answering most mistakes with "Invalid configuration: : Invalid input"; it now says what to change
  • Fixed the Ctrl+C hint on a background MCP task's question saying "cancel" when the second press leaves the question to answer later
  • Fixed pressing c to copy an MCP sign-in URL leaving a stray c in the paste field
  • Fixed Tab and Shift+Tab not moving between fields in an MCP server's input form, and a required field there keeping its tick after being emptied
  • Remote Control: Fixed a session disconnecting mid-reply when the server was briefly unavailable
  • Remote Control: Fixed the QR code in /remote-control being cut off in short terminal windows such as 80×24
  • Remote Control: Fixed terminal sessions showing as idle on your phone while background subagents were still running; Stop on your phone or the web now ends them together with the turn
  • Fixed Remote Control showing a session as running while it waited on a prompt that can only be answered in the terminal, and as idle when turned on while a tool was running
  • Fixed a reply in a remote session running again after a restart when Stop had been pressed while Claude Code was restarting
  • Fixed Stop in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions sometimes waiting for slow MCP servers to connect before taking effect
  • Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when a proxy answers an upload with its own HTTP 502, 504 or 520 to 524; the upload now gets a second try
  • Fixed claude.ai chats and Cowork tasks sometimes not sending a file after you chose "Send it" at the check for secret keys
  • Fixed claude.ai chats and Cowork tasks asking about a plugin file only because it holds a Word, Excel or other zip-type file; such files are now read for secret keys first
  • Fixed claude self-hosted-runner asking for new tokens nonstop when a refreshed token was already due, such as when the machine's clock runs ahead
  • Fixed /autofix-pr reporting a run as cancelled when its cloud session could not be stopped; it now links the session so you can stop it
  • Fixed /teleport hiding a session from its list in narrow terminals
  • Fixed artifact publishing refusing files in a background session's temporary folder
  • Fixed subagents whose disallowedTools lists Artifact still being offered artifact tools in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Claude calling a just-published artifact private when people with access to its folder can open it

items.title: RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
items.summary: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. To address VLM fragility, we further propose RoSci-Agent, a framework that employs a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline to vet premises before reasoning. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. RoSci-Agent achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the evaluated standalone VLMs. RoSci-Bench gives the multimodal reasoning community a common test of when models answer, request clarification, or reject a scientific question.

items.title: Open CDLM: A Benchmark and Library for Continuous Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Reliable comparisons of continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) require evaluating both model fit and the distribution of generated text. Two common practices leave this goal only partially addressed. Likelihood-based evaluation often reports a variational upper bound on discrete negative log-likelihood, whose slack can confound comparisons. Generated-sample-based evaluation commonly combines generative perplexity with within-sequence unigram entropy; both scores can remain favorable even when a sampler produces the same text on every draw. We introduce \textbf{Open CDLM}, a benchmark for evaluating CDLMs and their samplers, and describe the design of an accompanying open-source library to support reproducible comparisons. For likelihood-based evaluation, we clarify which comparisons of model fit are supported by reported perplexity bounds and how those conclusions depend on the evaluation procedure. For sample-based evaluation, we use \textit{Kernel Text Discrepancy} (\textbf{KTD}) to compare collections of generated and real texts, alongside diagnostics for diversity, validity, and coverage. In controlled OpenWebText experiments, replacing a collection of texts with copies of a single selected passage improves both conventional generation scores. MAUVE detects the resulting collapse, and its response to other perturbations depends on the text representation and the type of perturbation. This work marks the beginning of Open CDLM as an open-source project for CDLM research. We will maintain and extend the library over time and welcome contributions from the community.
